findings.claim: Under the default bitwarden tenant, `sec run` is a bare exec; the only export in bin/sec is BW_SESSION, while README/SECURITY/OPERATOR_MANUAL/completions promise secret injection into process memory.
findings.consequence: A `sec run -- terraform plan` job launches with zero vault secrets in its environment — running unauthenticated or against stray ambient .env values while reporting no error.

findings.claim: setup-keychain's else-branch writes the Bitwarden master password in plaintext to ~/.cache/bitwarden/master_pass whenever neither macOS security nor secret-tool exists (common stock Linux); get_master_password reads it back.
findings.consequence: On a libsecret-less box the vault-opening password rests on disk unencrypted where any backup/sync/dotfile archive of $HOME captures it — the exact leak SECURITY.md:16 marks as mitigated by keychain-only storage.

findings.claim: The master password is passed as an argv element to bw unlock (reached from "$0" unlock "$pass"), contradicting docs/SECURITY.md:13 which claims process-table snooping is mitigated via environment variables.
findings.consequence: With auto_rotate=true, an expired session makes sec get run `bw unlock <master-password>` — any local user reading ps/proc/<pid>/cmdline during that window recovers the master password in cleartext.

findings.quote: Single Source of Truth: Bitwarden Vault / bws
findings.claim: The controller never invokes bw/bws — SYNC_KEYS values are read solely from os.environ — yet the banner, README:86 and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:14 declare the vault the source.
findings.consequence: Rotating a key in Bitwarden changes nothing downstream until re-exported in the shell; sec sync pushes whatever stale env values are present to prod GCP/GitLab and exits 0 under a banner declaring Bitwarden authoritative.

findings.quote: Targets: GCP Secret Manager, GitLab Group Variables, Vercel Projects
findings.claim: Vercel appears only in this docstring — no sync_to_vercel, no VERCEL_* env, no Vercel call site anywhere in the repo; main() calls only sync_to_gcp_secret_manager and sync_to_gitlab_group.
findings.consequence: An operator told sec sync lands secrets in Vercel watches Vercel deployments keep stale/missing env vars forever, with sync exiting 0 and no error naming the missing target.

findings.claim: p.returncode is never inspected after communicate (only :81 checks a returncode), and communicate() is called with no timeout= and the file has no alarm/signal/setdefaulttimeout.
findings.consequence: A gcloud that exits non-zero (permission revoked, quota, wrong project) is silently treated as a successful write — and a gcloud that hangs wedges sec sync forever with the plaintext value held in the wedged process's stdin buffer.

findings.quote: print(f"    ✅ GCP Secret Manager: {secret_name} updated successfully.")
findings.claim: The success line executes unconditionally after the unchecked communicate().
findings.consequence: A failed gcloud secrets versions add is reported to the operator as 'updated successfully' and the run still exits 0 (F008), so cron/CI records 'secrets synced' while production keeps the stale key.

findings.claim: main() returns 0 after any push attempt: both sync_to_* swallow all exceptions (⚠️ notices at :110/:132), synced_count increments unconditionally, and the documented 0/1/2 contract is satisfied by attempting rather than by succeeding.
findings.consequence: 100% backend failure yields exit 0 plus a completion banner counting keys that were never written; a --yes CI caller cannot detect that no secret was actually stored, and partial state (key1 written, key2 failed, key3 never attempted) is never signalled.
findings.evidence: A11 (A10 rejected the counter wording; defect located in exit status)

findings.claim: urlopen is called with no timeout= and no socket.setdefaulttimeout exists anywhere in the file.
findings.consequence: A stalled gitlab.com connection hangs sec sync indefinitely instead of failing — remaining keys never attempted, stuck CI job holds its runner, operator must SIGKILL.

findings.claim: capture_output=True puts gcloud's stderr into the CalledProcessError, but the handler prints only str(e); the versions-add Popen's stderr=PIPE at :105 is never read either.
findings.consequence: The operator gets exit 0 (F008) plus a diagnostic line omitting gcloud's own reason (permission denied / API not enabled / project not found); triage requires re-running gcloud by hand outside the tool.

findings.claim: When stdin is not a TTY, read returns 1 at EOF and set -euo pipefail exits before any message is printed (same pattern at :161 for setup).
findings.consequence: The advertised systemd/cron/unattended deployment fails silently (exit 1, no message, no log) and bin/sec:94 discards even that via >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; an operator debugging an expired vault sees nothing at all.

findings.claim: cmd_apply has branches only for bw (:157) and op (:185); cmd_plan records detect_backend's value verbatim, and bws is detect_backend's first choice when `bws secret list` succeeds.
findings.consequence: For a bws-configured user `sec housekeep apply` executes zero mutations, then unconditionally rm -f's the plan file (:197) and prints the success banner — the reorganization never happens, the plan is destroyed, and success is reported.

findings.claim: op's flag is --tags (empty value removes all tags), so this revert command fails with an unknown-flag error that the redirect+|| true discards; original tags were never captured by plan anyway; then cmd_revert rm -f's $LATEST_SNAPSHOT (:250) and prints success.
findings.consequence: 1Password items stay unrestored, the operator is told the revert succeeded, the only rollback record is destroyed, and a subsequent sec housekeep revert reports 'No pre-apply snapshot found'; the same wrong --tag flag is used by cmd_apply at :193, so op housekeep apply edits silently fail the same way.

findings.claim: The plan file is created at default umask (0644) and only chmod 600 at apply time (:153); this script's mkdir -p "$CACHE_DIR" (:8) never enforces SECURITY.md:24's documented 0700 cache-dir mode (chmod 700 exists only at bw-session-keeper:14).
findings.consequence: On a multi-user host before the first apply — and on any box where bw-session-keeper has never run — the full inventory of secret names, UUIDs and target folders (usernames can embed via sec-classify.py:71) sits world-readable under a 0755 directory, contradicting the documented permission architecture.

findings.claim: Any jq failure — a transaction log truncated by an interrupted jq -n write, or a schema mismatch — becomes an empty result via || echo "".
findings.consequence: --undo reports 'zero created items' and exits 0 while the secrets it was meant to delete remain in the destination vault.

findings.claim: The append is unconditional: items skipped because $val was empty (infisical/vault branches never call trap_error) are logged with id "" and counted in migrated_count; TX_FILE's only writes are this log's tail (:201) and trap_error (:131) — there is no shell trap for SIGINT/SIGKILL.
findings.consequence: --apply reports a completed migration for secrets never written (and --undo later issues a delete for an empty id); after a hard kill mid-apply no transaction file exists at all, so orphaned items are untrackable and --undo answers 'No active migration transaction log found' — the advertised single-command rollback is unavailable exactly when needed.
findings.evidence: C10 (+P7/P10 walk: no trap statement in file)

findings.claim: classify_item never reads login.password/login.username/login.totp — an AKIA key stored the normal way (item password field) scores general/50 via fallback while the same key in .notes scores cloud/aws/71; a null login.uris[].uri also makes the join raise, dropping the item to the confidence-0 fallback.
findings.consequence: A live AWS access key in the standard location is reported as 'general' and sec housekeep apply moves it into a folder named general — out of cloud/aws — with no warning at any stage, so an operator auditing for AWS material never sees it.

findings.claim: The token iam is claimed only by cloud/aws, so GCP's own identity string (iam.gserviceaccount.com) scores AWS and wins ties because CATEGORY_WEIGHTS declares cloud/aws first; cloud/gcp's rules know nothing of service_account/gserviceaccount.com.
findings.consequence: A GCP service-account credential is classified cloud/aws (verified: reasons [token:iam]) and housekeep apply files GCP credentials under an AWS tag/folder — the wrong cloud entirely.

findings.claim: The set) inner case has arms only for bitwarden|bw (:466), 1pass|op (:531) and bws (:537) — no vault, no infisical, no keychain, and no *) arm.
findings.consequence: `sec vault set K V` / `sec infisical set K V` / `sec keychain set K V` skip every arm, fall to esac, print nothing and exit 0 — a silent no-op success on a secret-write path (any failed op/bws create inside the implemented arms exits 0 the same way).
findings.evidence: F6 (B4 confirmed the no-failure-branch half; B3 rejected the regex line as the location)

findings.claim: No folder/tenant/org scoping exists anywhere in get: :337 searches the whole account, :340 takes the first arbitrary match, and on a miss :351 dumps every item and returns the first field named $key anywhere.
findings.consequence: Two tenants' identically-named items are resolved by array position, so one tenant's secret can be returned to a caller targeting another tenant — silently, exit 0; combined with D13's hardcoded 8-alias prefix router, a documented custom [work] section is not routable at all (usage, exit 0).

findings.claim: The sync arm is if -x then exec … fi with no else and no message; when the controller is absent/non-executable the script falls through to esac and exits 0 with no output.
findings.consequence: On a tree where the controller lost its exec bit or was never copied, `sec sync` silently succeeds having pushed zero keys — the suite itself predicts this at tests/test_install.sh:73 ('would fall through silently') yet only asserts -x in the installer path.
findings.evidence: F7 (B6 rejected the guard line when the file is present — the defect is the absent else-branch)

findings.quote: subcmds="get set run housekeep migrate unlock rotate setup-keychain completion --help -h --version -v"
findings.claim: sync is dispatched (:562) and documented in usage (:141) but absent from ALL five completion surfaces — completions/_sec (grep -c sync = 0), zsh (:179), bash (:237), fish (:272-284), ps1 (:294).
findings.consequence: sec syn<TAB> completes to nothing in every shell, so the one command that performs production writes is the one command users cannot discover by tab-completion, and no --dry-run/--yes completion is offered for it.
findings.evidence: B9+F5 (E18 rejected _sec:3 as the location — file body is valid, the absence is the defect)

findings.quote: echo "  sec completion {zsh|bash|ps1}            Generate shell autocompletion scripts"
findings.claim: usage() offers three shells while the router implements fish (:261) and README:92 documents `sec completion fish`.
findings.consequence: A user following `sec --help` is told the shipped fish completion does not exist (verified working, exit 0), while README's hand-maintained copy has already drifted the other way.

findings.claim: eval of op signin stdout is 1Password's own documented idiom, BUT the enclosing guard (:116) tests `op account list` — accounts configured, not session validity.
findings.consequence: An expired 1Password session is never re-authenticated: sec 1pass get misreports 'Secret not found' while sec 1pass set exits 0 storing nothing — silent false success on the 1pass write path (eval injection risk itself rejected as upstream idiom).
findings.evidence: B2 (original eval-injection framing rejected; guard-scope defect stands)

findings.claim: Provider stderr is discarded (same pattern at :337) so a failing bw yields empty input; the user then sees :437 "Error: Secret '$key' not found in tenant '$TARGET_TENANT'." exit 1.
findings.consequence: A network outage, expired session or locked vault is reported as a missing secret with exit 1 — the operator hunts for a key that exists, and 0 timeouts/retries exist anywhere in bin/ to distinguish the cases.

findings.claim: The run fallback re-parses already-tokenized argv as PowerShell source (contrast bash's literal exec "$@"), and $args holds only tokens past the three declared positionals — `sec.ps1 run terraform plan` never runs terraform at all as documented.
findings.consequence: Any wrapper forwarding caller-supplied arguments through sec.ps1 run runs the tail as PowerShell (`;`, `&`, backticks, $(…)) instead of passing it literally — argv becomes a code sink; and the documented run idiom is simply broken.

findings.quote: - `bin/sec.ps1`: Native Windows PowerShell wrapper for the same subcommand surface.
findings.claim: sec.ps1 implements only get/set/housekeep/migrate/run (its own default prints the 5-command usage); sync/unlock/rotate/setup-keychain/completion and the whole tenant-prefix grammar are absent.
findings.consequence: On Windows-native, `sec.ps1 sync` prints usage and exits 0 — a silent no-op success for the production-push command with no way to reach the --dry-run/--yes guards; tenant-targeted commands silently resolve to the default backend instead of erroring.
findings.evidence: D5 (E17: the ps1 usage string itself is accurate — the doc claim is the defect)

findings.claim: No inject) or audit) case exists anywhere in bin/sec; the row enumerates 4 of the 15 dispatched names, omitting sync/set/housekeep/migrate/setup-keychain/completion.
findings.consequence: A reader treating the architecture doc as API reference tries `sec audit`, hits the *) usage fallback and gets help on stdout with exit 0 — a scripted caller captures the usage block as its 'value' and is told the call succeeded.

findings.quote: - `bin/bw-session-keeper`: Daemon process maintaining encrypted Bitwarden unlock sessions.
findings.claim: No daemon-install code exists anywhere (no launchctl/systemctl/crontab/cron in bin/); save_session writes the raw session key to plaintext ~/.cache/bitwarden/session, and README:13 additionally promises 1Password sessions kept alive — no code exists for that either.
findings.consequence: Nothing runs between commands, so the session key expires and every subsequent sec get degrades to an interactive unlock prompt — background keep-alive and 'encrypted sessions' never happen as documented.

findings.quote: Bitwarden/bws source of truth pushed to GCP Secret Manager, GitLab group CI/CD variables, Vercel projects.
findings.claim: Neither Vercel nor the Bitwarden-as-source claim matches the code (see F004, F005): the controller reads os.environ only.
findings.consequence: Three surfaces of the same feature disagree (doc, banner, code); an operator auditing sync coverage from the doc concludes Vercel projects are kept in sync when zero Vercel writes have ever occurred.

findings.quote: HashiCorp Vault, and AWS Secrets Manager.
findings.claim: No AWS backend exists anywhere (no aws in the tenant regex, no invocation in get/set/migrate); README:5 widens the same claim to GCP Secret Manager, Unix Pass and OS Keychains — 4 of 9 advertised backends do nothing, and keychain (accepted by :65) has no get/set branch.
findings.consequence: `sec aws get KEY` / `sec pass get KEY` print usage and exit 0 (automation captures help text as the secret value), while `sec keychain get` exits 1 'not found' forever and `sec keychain set` exits 0 storing nothing.

findings.claim: False on the face of the code: sec-organizer shells out to jq unguarded (no `command -v jq` anywhere in bin/), classify/controller need python3, install.sh checks neither, and README has no prerequisites section — independently of the dead-backend claims in F031.
findings.consequence: Install reports 'installed successfully' on a box without jq, then sec housekeep dies at the first jq invocation mid-plan after the vault was already read — users diagnose a broken tool instead of a missing package.

findings.quote: Master passwords stored in macOS Keychain (`security`) or Linux Secret Service (`secret-tool`).
findings.claim: The threat-matrix row declares keychain-only storage while the code's third path (F002) writes plaintext whenever neither binary exists; SECURITY.md:11 'never written to disk' and OPERATOR_MANUAL:11 'exclusively in secure OS Keychains' repeat the same gap.
findings.consequence: A reader of the security documentation is told the plaintext-password threat class is closed on Linux, so no compensating control (restrict HOME perms, avoid unattended setup-keychain on headless) is ever applied.

findings.claim: The reference has six entries; grep for sync and for completion in the whole document returns 0 hits — two dispatched commands, including the only one with blast-radius controls, are undocumented.
findings.consequence: An operator consulting the flag reference to run a production sync cannot find --dry-run, --yes, the exit codes 0/1/2, or even the command's existence, and must fall through to the one-line help.

findings.quote: You can target any tenant directly by prefixing its section name before the subcommand:
findings.claim: Prefix routing is a hardcoded eight-alias regex (bin/sec:65), not anything read from sec.conf — a user-added [work] section is not routable.
findings.consequence: A custom tenant section is treated as the subcommand: `sec work get KEY` falls to *) usage and exits 0 — no secret, and CI sees success — so the documented 'any tenant' promise is false for every non-default section.

findings.quote: sec sync                                 Central Secret Sync Engine: Sync Bitwarden secrets to GCP & GitLab
findings.claim: README's command reference still documents bare sec sync with no flags, while the shipped usage is `sec sync [--dry-run|--yes]` with preview/confirm semantics added by the issue-#3 fix.
findings.consequence: The one command that pushes secrets to production is documented to users without its safety flags; a reader never learns --dry-run exists, so the guard ships while the primary user-facing surface still reads as 'one command, no preview'.

findings.claim: The vault branch references $item_name which is only assigned inside the bitwarden/1pass branches; under set -u the line aborts (verified: 'item_name: unbound variable', exit 1); with vault absent it dies rc=127 instead.
findings.consequence: The one README example demonstrating non-Bitwarden field-level retrieval never returns a secret — it crashes with an internal bash error rather than a diagnosable 'vault backend unavailable'.

findings.claim: In piped mode SCRIPT_DIR resolves to the caller's cwd (BASH_SOURCE[0]:-. fallback at :17), so a directory containing its own bin/sec skips the clone and installs that foreign file.
findings.consequence: A `curl | bash` run from any directory containing bin/sec (sibling project, ~/bin/sec) silently installs a foreign file as your sec first on PATH — reproduced: marker file installed, then aborted mid-copy leaving a half-install.

findings.claim: A git-tracked project config hardcodes an absolute path into a different repository, unconditionally fetches a live GitLab PAT into an sh -c string whose target binary is path-controlled with no integrity pin.
findings.consequence: On any other machine or clone — or once the hub checkout moves — the hyer MCP server can never start (silently wrong downstream), and a PR rewriting the exec target exfiltrates the PAT the moment a maintainer approves the project MCP server.
findings.evidence: E9 (portability half confirmed; original path-injection of SYNC_KEYS rejected as A8 — not attacker-controlled)

findings.quote: `AGENTS.md` §1's Session Scoping and Breach Protocol guidance apply
findings.claim: AGENTS.md §1 contains no such text — it lives in methodology/tiers.md:44/:49 (the hub's own copy now words it that way); the §6/two-tier cross-ref at :40 points at Credentials & Blast Radius instead of methodology/credentials.md:14; the free-tier principle claim at :9-10 has no AGENTS.md hit; and the scale-to-zero MUST (:19-22) has no IaC to check.
findings.consequence: An adopter told these rules apply regardless is sent to sections that do not contain them — the pack reads as verified policy while its anchors are unresolvable.

findings.claim: No code ever reads any cli key (get_cfg_val called only for global/default_backend at :61 and <tenant>/auto_rotate at :78; other scripts never parse sec.conf); [global] auto_rotate is equally unread; and the parser's regex match on the raw line means a commented-out key is still honored.
findings.consequence: A user setting `cli = /opt/custom/bw` gets a silently ignored setting while sec keeps hardcoding provider binaries — both the 'configure' and the 'disable' affordances of the documented config are broken (README:50-70 repeats the inert keys).

findings.claim: Git index mode is 100644 for this suite while both siblings are 100755 (same shebang); worktree matches.
findings.consequence: ./tests/test_sentinel.sh fails with Permission denied, so a contributor or hook globbing executable test files silently runs 2 of 3 suites while appearing to succeed — the third is skipped by the shell's exec check, not by an assertion, so no red result is ever produced.

findings.quote: - **Last updated**: 2026-10-08 (truth-up pass: dead GitLab CI removed,
findings.claim: The file's most recent content edit is commit 4b7e3d0 on 2026-10-09 (registry-count truth-up); the stamp still says 2026-10-08.
findings.consequence: Anyone judging the doc's currency from the stamp gets the wrong last-modified date for a file that changed the next day.

findings.quote: if grep -q "secrets versions add gemini-api-key" "$CANARY" 2>/dev/null; then
findings.claim: Assertions pin only key names: zero occurrences of sublime-flux-504502-k3 / GCP_PROJECT / at-tech-io / GITLAB_GROUP anywhere in tests/ — the write destination the implementation defaults (controller :14-15) is never asserted.
findings.consequence: Circular pass: a typo'd/renamed/copied-from-another-repo default GCP project or GitLab group id makes all 18 assertions green while sec sync --yes writes production secrets into the wrong project.
findings.evidence: F1 (E6: the canary pattern itself is correct — the defect is what it does NOT assert)

findings.quote: for f in sec bw-session-keeper sec-organizer sec-classify.py sec-migrator sec-sync-controller.py; do
findings.claim: This -x existence loop is the ONLY occurrence of four of those scripts in tests/ — none is ever executed (no behavior assertion anywhere).
findings.consequence: 791 lines of runtime code (organizer 259 + migrator 207 + keeper 173 + classify 152) ship with zero behavioral coverage — sec housekeep/migrate/auto-rotation regressions pass every green run (E5: the loop itself correctly matches install.sh's cp set — the defect is existence-only).
findings.evidence: F2 (E5 rejected loop-completeness as the defect framing)

findings.claim: The suites invoke bin/sec only twice, both --help (test_install.sh:64, test_sync_guard.sh:101) — only the -h arm (bin/sec:160) ever runs; get/set/run/sync/housekeep/migrate arms and 42 nested backend arms are never exercised, and || true swallows --help's exit code.
findings.consequence: The core secret read/write/inject surface — the product's reason to exist — is verified only that it doesn't appear in --help text; any regression there is invisible to every gate this repo has.

findings.claim: The gcloud shim hardcodes exit 0; asserted exit codes cover only the documented 0/2/1/0/0/2 paths — no test ever makes a backend command fail.
findings.consequence: The controller's failure-path exit code (F006/F007/F008's whole defect class) is unasserted, so a regression that returns 0 on total backend failure stays green forever.

findings.quote: items_json="$(op item list --format=json 2>/dev/null | jq '[.[] | {id: .id, name: .title, tags: .tags}]' || echo "[]")"
findings.claim: The op projection strips to id/name/tags (bws at :63 strips to id/name only) before the single classify call at :88 — notes/uris/fields never reach the classifier for those backends; apply contains zero classification logic and replays plan-time targets.
findings.consequence: Classification quality silently differs per backend (byte-identical secrets bin differently in bw vs op), and plan→apply executes months-old decisions with no staleness re-check before the vault write.

findings.claim: GEMINI.md does not exist at repo root (mechanical ls); settings carry no excludeTools/hooks — clean on the risk axis, dead on the config axis.
findings.consequence: Gemini CLI is configured to load a documentation file that is not in the repo — dead config surface and a misleading hint about the declared doc set.

findings.claim: No log file is ever created anywhere (grep of bin/ for log emitters: only .login.password false positives; no tracked *.log).
findings.consequence: The ignore rule is policy against a non-existent emitter while the actual failure surface (F006-F010, F011) is transient stdout/stderr only — if logging is ever added every log lands untracked, in a repo whose whole subject is secret handling.

findings.claim: install.sh copies seven files into ~/.local/bin and never copies LICENSE (grep -n LICENSE install.sh: no matches); MIT requires the notice in all copies.
findings.consequence: Every installation produced by the documented one-liner and manual-clone paths is a copy of the Software omitting the required copyright/permission notice — direct non-compliance with the license the repo claims.

findings.claim: The opted-in packs list names three packs while the disk holds five — packs/compliance-baseline and packs/human-team-coordination are present but never declared (mechanical ls vs list).
findings.consequence: AGENTS.md §2 routes every boot through this list, so a compliance checklist fully present in the tree is never loaded by any agent — present-but-not-declared implies coverage that no session acts on.

findings.claim: grep -n version install.sh: no matches — zero version or dependency checks (jq, python3, gcloud, bw, op, bws never referenced); the PATH toolchain is entirely unpinned.
findings.consequence: Install 'succeeds' on a host missing jq/python3 and breaks at runtime instead of install; the next breaking bw/op/bws major rewrites flags under a script with no minimum-version gate — fleet-wide silent failure for a tool invoked against production secret stores.

findings.quote: (directory absent — mechanical: ls .github/workflows fails; git tag -l empty; no Makefile/pyproject/package.json/pytest.ini)
findings.claim: No CI, no tags, no releases, no coverage tooling; the only pre-existing quality gate is a machine-local untracked hook whose Step 5 structurally cannot run tests/*.sh (open issue #2, hub-side).
findings.consequence: No automated check of any kind blocks a broken commit to main; the suite passes today only because a human remembered to run it — the next push goes straight to the branch that README's curl|bash feeds every user.

findings.claim: Issue #1's checklist required re-syncing packs/ too; at the adoption SHA 736000d, 7 of 9 pack files still differ (solo-founder-governance local v1.2.0 8-persona vs hub v1.4.0 9-persona) and the v5.28.0..v5.39.1 changelog review has no recorded evidence anywhere.
findings.consequence: The opted-in governance pack that names this repo's final approver is silently two minor versions stale — the pack's newest persona obligations never reach any agent that boots this repo, while the tracker shows the work finished.
findings.evidence: byte-diff vs 736000d (E14: heading itself internally consistent — defect is the closed checklist scope, not the heading)
